text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Apartment prices in inner-city Stockholm rose steeply this spring and have now reached levels higher than the records set at the end of the 1980s. Flats and houses in the Ostermalm area are the most expensive with a third costing more than a million crowns, according to industry statistics.

- The Finance department is considering lowering the contributions people have to make to sickness benefits but raising contributions to pensions and unemployment payments. The department estimates the sickness benefit system will see a surplus of 20 billion crowns in 1998, according to internal departmental documents.
- A worker with a job in the private sector earned an average of 97.90 crowns an hour in May this year which was a rise of 3.4 percent compared to May in 1996, according to Statistics Sweden.

- Overseas interest in the Stockholm bourse increased in June with net export of shares reaching 7.5 billion crowns, the first time since Novmeber 1996 that overseas buying has exceeeded the amount of shares sold back into Sweden, the central bank said. The hottest shares were international engineer ABB and drugs major Astra.
- For the first time more people have moved to Sweden as normal citizens than refugees, according to a study by the newspaper. Immigration to Sweden has fallen sharply but even more so for refugees.
- King Carl XVI Gustaf will visit Bosnia next month.
- Prime Minister Goran Persson could travel to Poland next week to offer his support after the massive flooding there and see if Sweden can offer more assistance.

- Sweden's JP Bank posted a surprisingly weak profit of 14.3 million crowns against 39 million crowns in the first half of 1996 but this did not knock the share price. Earnings per share after tax were 0.86 crowns against 2.15 crowns. Total earnings fell by 41 percent to 59.9 million crowns while staff costs fell 28 percent to 32.4 million crowns.

- Petrochemical group Borealis in Stenungsund is on its way to a billion crown profit this year. With an investment of 3.5 billion crowns the company hopes to become one of the world's 10 most effective petrochemical makers.
- The business cycle and reduced building has hit furniture makers in the city of Tibro in southern Sweden hard.

- The Swedish government will save far less than the one billion crowns it had estimated through drug market reforms that came into effect at the beginning of the year. The most noticeable effect is that people are buying less and cheaper drugs. In the first half of 1997 drug sales over the counter fell by 600 million crowns to 8.6 billion crowns, according to the chemist monopoly, Apoteksbolaget.
- Stockholm's A-list could see a world leading forestry consulting group listing this autumn with Finland's Jaakko Poyry thinking of listing in both Stockholm and Helsinki.
